chapter_title: Introduction to Solidity and Development Environment

screens.title: Introduction to Solidity and Development Environment
screens.subtitle: Learn Solidity basics, the EVM model, and how to compile and deploy a simple contract using Remix.

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you'll meet Solidity, the language used to write rules that live on the Ethereum blockchain, and the runtime that executes those rules, the Ethereum Virtual Machine. You'll also learn how to use the Remix browser IDE to write, compile, and deploy a small Greeter contract. Knowing how Solidity maps to EVM bytecode is essential because every operation consumes gas, and gas affects security, user cost, and design choices. We will practice writing a constructor that initializes state, a read-only getter that uses the view modifier, and a mutating setter that requires a transaction. By the end you'll be able to create a new. sol file in Remix, choose a compatible compiler version, deploy to the JavaScript VM, and call functions to observe changes in contract state. A practical mindset helps: think about which variables must be stored forever and which can stay local to a function; that distinction drives gas cost. As you begin, ask yourself: what data truly needs persistence on-chain and what can live off-chain to save gas?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Solidity defines on-chain logic and the EVM executes it; using Remix you can quickly iterate, deploy, and observe how state, gas, and compiler choices shape your smart contract behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Introduction
Introduction to Solidity and Remix
A practical start: write, compile, deploy.

Solidity is a contract-oriented, statically typed language that compiles to EVM bytecode. Remix is a browser IDE that removes local setup friction so you can iterate quickly. In this lesson set you'll see how state, gas, and compiler versions influence contract behavior and cost.

In this lesson
Solidity role
EVM model
Remix walk-through

You'll implement a Greeter contract, compile with a matching pragma, and deploy to the JavaScript VM to observe calls that are free to run off-chain and transactions that change state and cost gas.

Explore Key Topics
Solidity basics — types, functions, constructors.
Remix IDE — file explorer, compiler, deploy panel.
Gas & state — when changes cost and why it matters.
Interactive Concept View
Solidity

Contract-oriented language. Declares state and functions that compile to EVM bytecode.

EVM

Executes bytecode for every node. Gas measures computation and storage cost.

Remix

Browser IDE that lets you edit .sol files, select compiler versions, and deploy to a simulated VM to test read-only and state-changing functions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how Solidity fits into the Ethereum stack, configure and use Remix for quick development, and write a simple contract that demonstrates state and view functions. You'll learn to recognize fundamental types such as unsigned integers, booleans, addresses, and byte arrays, and to choose the right type for balances and identifiers. You will also understand the difference between state variables that persist on-chain and local variables that exist only during execution, and why changing state requires a transaction and gas. Each objective includes a small example or mnemonic to make the skill transferable: for instance, you will practice deploying the Greeter contract with an initial message to see the constructor run, and you will call a view function to observe a free, off-chain read. These hands-on skills reduce friction and make it easier to prototype secure, gas-aware contracts.

keyIdea.title: Practical outcomes
keyIdea.text: Set up Remix, compile with a matching pragma, deploy to the local JavaScript VM, and reason about gas and storage when designing simple contracts.

screens.title: What is Solidity and why it matters
screens.subtitle: A contract-oriented language that compiles to EVM bytecode

narration.text: Solidity is a high-level, contract-oriented programming language created to express the rules and state of decentralized applications running on Ethereum. When you write a contract in Solidity, you are defining a set of persistent variables and functions that nodes will execute using the Ethereum Virtual Machine. The key claim to remember is that Solidity source is not what lives on-chain; it compiles into bytecode that the EVM runs. That mapping affects everything: gas costs, security boundaries, and upgrade strategies. For a concrete example, consider a token contract that stores balances as state. Each transfer modifies state and therefore consumes gas; the same logic expressed inefficiently will simply cost more to execute. A common misconception is thinking Solidity behaves like standard server-side languages; it does not. There is no private server memory, and every persistent change is globally visible and costly. Practice: open a simple contract with a state variable and a setter to see how changing that variable requires a transaction in Remix. Key takeaway: design with persistence cost in mind and prefer minimal, well-typed state for safety and lower gas.

keyIdea.title: Solidity → EVM bytecode
keyIdea.text: Solidity expresses contracts; the compiler produces bytecode executed by the EVM and charged gas per operation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Solidity Defined
Definition

Solidity is a statically typed, contract-oriented language whose source compiles into EVM bytecode. This bytecode is stored on-chain and executed by nodes, with each operation consuming gas.

Claim: Persistence costs money — every state write uses gas.
Example: A simple balance update triggers a storage write and incurs gas proportional to storage change.
Misconception check: Contracts are not private server code; state is visible and immutable once recorded.
Key Takeaway

Design minimal persistent state. Fewer writes means lower gas and fewer attack surfaces.

Analogy

Think of Solidity as a recipe and EVM bytecode as the packaged meal. The recipe tells you what to do, but the packaged meal is what the network consumes and pays to prepare.

Concrete example
State variable: uint256 balance; Setter: transfer function that updates balances and requires a transaction.
Pro tip
Avoid unnecessary state writes. Compute values in memory or off-chain when possible.

screens.title: Compilation to EVM and gas implications
screens.subtitle: How source code becomes bytecode and why each operation costs gas

narration.text: Compilation is the bridge between human-readable Solidity and machine-executable EVM bytecode. The compiler reads your source, enforces type rules, and outputs a binary format that the EVM understands. Each Solidity construct maps to low-level operations that consume gas when executed. For example, reading memory is cheap compared to storing a value in contract storage, which is one of the most expensive operations. When you compile and deploy a contract, the resulting bytecode is stored on-chain; deployment itself is a transaction that consumes gas proportional to the code size and initialization work done in the constructor. A concrete practice is to measure gas when you change a uint state variable versus when you compute a temporary variable in a function; the former writes to persistent storage and uses significantly more gas. A common misconception is assuming the compiler optimizes away costly instructions; while compilers help, you must write gas-conscious code, prefer efficient types like uint256 for arithmetic, and avoid redundant storage writes. Think ahead: the compiler turns intent into cost, so design contracts to minimize unnecessary persistence and heavy loops. Compilation to EVM and gas implications means every compiled instruction in bytecode consumes gas; storage writes are especially expensive and should be minimized.. In practical terms, how source code becomes bytecode and why each operation costs gas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas is the execution meter
keyIdea.text: Every compiled instruction in bytecode consumes gas; storage writes are especially expensive and should be minimized.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Compilation & Gas
Compilation Steps
  1. Source code is parsed and type-checked by the compiler.
  2. Compiler emits EVM bytecode and an ABI for function calls.
  3. Deployment stores bytecode on-chain; constructors run during deployment.
Why gas differs
  • Memory reads are cheap; storage writes are expensive.
  • Loops with storage writes compound cost per iteration.
  • Contract size increases deployment gas.
Concrete example
Compare: Setting state variable balance = balance + 1 costs storage write gas. Computing temp = balance + 1 and returning it without writing is cheaper.
Common mistake
Assuming compiler will remove redundant writes. Always review and avoid unnecessary assignments to state.
Key Takeaway

Measure gas for common operations and refactor to reduce storage writes and heavy loops.

screens.title: Pragma directive and compiler selection
screens.subtitle: Why matching the pragma to the compiler matters for consistent behavior

narration.text: The pragma directive at the top of a Solidity file declares the compiler versions that are allowed to compile your code. This matters because Solidity evolves and language features or safety checks can change between versions. For example, using a caret range like caret zero point eight dot zero allows any compiler from that minor release upwards, but you must be careful to avoid unintentionally compiling with a version that introduces breaking changes. In practice, match the compiler in Remix to your pragma so the compiled bytecode and behavior match your expectations. A concrete example: pragma solidity caret zero point eight dot zero ensures you get the overflow checks introduced in 0.8.0, which revert on overflow instead of wrapping. A common misconception is that the pragma is merely documentation; it is enforced by the compiler and affects compilation errors and runtime safety. When deploying to production, pinning to a narrow version range reduces risk. Key takeaway: set a clear pragma, confirm the compiler in Remix, and recompile if you change versions to avoid surprising behavior. Pragma directive and compiler selection means a matching pragma ensures the compiler enforces expected language rules and safety behaviors; always verify the compiler version before compiling.. In practical terms, why matching the pragma to the compiler matters for consistent behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pragma controls compiler compatibility
keyIdea.text: A matching pragma ensures the compiler enforces expected language rules and safety behaviors; always verify the compiler version before compiling.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Pragma & Compiler
Pragma directive

The pragma line communicates supported compiler versions, for example: pragma solidity ^0.8.0; Pinning to a suitable range prevents accidental compilation with incompatible versions.

Example: ^0.8.0 enables overflow checks added in 0.8.x series.
Practice: In Remix, select the Solidity Compiler plugin and set the version to one that satisfies your pragma before compiling.
Misconception: The pragma is not just documentation — it guides compilation choices and warnings.
Quick checklist
  • Set pragma in source to the intended range.
  • Select matching compiler version in Remix.
  • Recompile after version changes and re-run tests.
Key Takeaway

Confirm the compiler version matches your pragma to preserve safety guarantees and avoid breaking changes.

screens.title: Contract structure: pragma, contract, constructor, functions
screens.subtitle: Anatomy of a .sol file and the role of each section

narration.text: A typical Solidity file begins with the pragma directive, followed by license identifiers and then contract declarations. The contract block is the primary unit and contains state variables, constructor logic, and functions. State variables declared at the contract level persist on-chain. The constructor runs once during deployment to initialize those variables. Functions can be marked view to indicate they read state without modifying it, or left as mutating functions that change state and cost gas. For example, a Greeter contract uses a string state variable to store a greeting, a constructor to initially set it, a view getter to return it without gas, and a setter that updates it and therefore requires a transaction. A misconception to avoid is treating the constructor like an ordinary function; it only runs during deployment and cannot be called later. Practice by creating a small file with pragma, a contract named Greeter, a constructor that accepts an initial message, a getter with the view specifier, and a setter that modifies the stored greeting. The structure maps directly to lifecycle and cost: initialization at deploy time, reads that are free off-chain, and writes that consume gas.

keyIdea.title: File anatomy matters
keyIdea.text: Pragma ensures compiler compatibility; contract defines persistent state; constructor initializes; view functions read, setters write and cost gas.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Contract Structure
Typical .sol anatomy
Pragma: selects compiler versions.
Contract: declares state and functions.
Constructor: runs once at deployment for initialization.
Functions: view reads are gas-free off-chain; setters write state and cost gas.
Misconception: Constructor can be called later — false. It only executes during deployment.
Key Takeaway

Map file sections to lifecycle: deploy-time initialization, read-only observations, and transactional updates.

Concrete example: Greeter
State:
string public greeting;
Constructor:
constructor(string memory initialGreeting) { greeting = initialGreeting; }
Functions:
getGreeting() public view returns (string memory)
setGreeting(string memory newGreeting) public

screens.title: Fundamental data types: uint, int, bool, address, bytes, string
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right type for correctness and cost

narration.text: Solidity provides several core types you will use frequently. Unsigned integers, or uint variants, hold non-negative numbers and are the common choice for token balances. Signed integers, or int, can represent negative values but are rarely used for quantities that must never be negative. Booleans store true or false. The address type holds a 20-byte Ethereum address and allows checks and transfers tied to accounts. Bytes come in fixed sized forms, like bytes32, and dynamic bytes for arbitrary binary data; string is a dynamic UTF-8 sequence for human-readable text but is expensive to store. A concrete example: use uint256 for token balances to avoid negative values; using int256 could open logical errors. A common misconception is that smaller integer sizes always save gas; while sometimes true, using non-standard sizes may add packing complexity — uint256 is most common and well-optimized. When storing user identifiers or contract addresses, use address; when storing textual metadata sparingly, use string or store off-chain and reference with a hash. Key takeaway: pick types that express intent and minimize on-chain storage cost. Fundamental data types: uint, int, bool, address, bytes, string means use uint for non-negative quantities, address for accounts, bytes/string for data, and prefer efficient sizes to balance cost and clarity.. In practical terms, choosing the right type for correctness and cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Type selection matters
keyIdea.text: Use uint for non-negative quantities, address for accounts, bytes/string for data, and prefer efficient sizes to balance cost and clarity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Data Types
Type Reference
uint / uint256 — unsigned integer for balances and counts.
int / int256 — signed integer when negative values are required.
bool — true or false flags for logic branches.
address — 20-byte Ethereum address for accounts and contracts.
bytes / bytes32 — binary data, fixed or dynamic.
string — UTF-8 text, costly to store on-chain.
Comparison: When to use which
Balances: uint256 — never negative.
Flags: bool — simple true/false checks.
Identity: address — for ownership and transfers.
Data blobs: bytes32 or bytes for binary; string only if user-facing text is necessary.
Common misconception: Using int for balances avoids negatives — actually it allows negatives and can introduce logic errors. Use uint for non-negative quantities.
Key Takeaway

Choose types by intent: correctness first, gas efficiency second. Prefer uint256 for balances and address for accounts.

screens.title: State variables vs local variables
screens.subtitle: Understanding persistence, storage costs, and lifetime

narration.text: State and local variables are fundamental to contract behavior and cost. State variables are declared at contract level and are stored permanently on the blockchain; changing them requires a transaction and consumes gas. Local variables are created inside functions and live only during execution; they exist in memory or on the stack and do not persist after the function returns. For example, in a counter contract, declaring counter as a state variable means each increment must be a transaction that writes to storage. If you create a temporary variable inside a function to compute a value for immediate use, it won't cost storage gas. A common mistake is to perform extra writes to state when a computed value would suffice; this increases cost and attack surface. Concrete exercise: in Remix try two versions of a function — one that writes a computed value to a state variable and one that returns the computed value without storing it. Observe gas differences when you call each. Key takeaway: minimize state writes and leverage local variables and view functions when persistence is not required.

keyIdea.title: Scope influences cost
keyIdea.text: State variables persist and cost gas to change; local variables are temporary and cheaper. Prefer local computation when possible.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › State vs Local
State variables

Declared at the contract level and stored on-chain. Example: uint256 public counter; Changing it triggers a transaction and storage write.

Cost note: Storage writes are among the most expensive EVM operations.
Local variables

Declared inside functions and exist only during execution. Use memory and stack to compute values without persisting them.

Practice: Compute tempValue = counter + 1 and return it instead of assigning back to counter to avoid storage cost.
Check your understanding
Example A: increment() writes to state — requires gas.
Example B: calculate() returns a value without writing — cheaper for callers.
Key Takeaway

Avoid unnecessary state updates. Use local variables for temporary computations and view functions for free reads.

screens.title: Greeter contract: code walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Read, compile, deploy — a guided example using Remix

narration.text: Let's walk through the Greeter contract to see these concepts in action. The contract declares a state variable greeting to store a message. The constructor accepts an initial message and assigns it to greeting; because constructors run only at deployment, this is how we initialize on-chain state. The getGreeting function is marked view and returns the greeting without modifying state, so calling it from an off-chain context costs no gas. The setGreeting function updates greeting and therefore requires a transaction. A concrete lab step: create Greeter. sol in Remix, paste the provided code, ensure pragma matches the compiler, and compile. Then deploy to the JavaScript VM with a constructor argument like "Hello Cohortia Learners!" and observe the deployed contract. Call getGreeting to confirm the initial text, then call setGreeting with a new message to see a transaction in the Remix console and a change in state when you call getGreeting again. A common misconception is expecting view functions to cost gas when called from the interface — they do not if called off-chain. Key takeaway: this simple contract demonstrates initialization, read-only calls, and state modifications with gas implications.

keyIdea.title: Greeter demonstrates lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Constructor initializes state at deployment; view functions read for free off-chain; setters change state and cost gas.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Greeter Walkthrough
Code (paste into Greeter.sol)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Greeter {
    string public greeting;

    constructor(string memory _initialGreeting) {
        greeting = _initialGreeting;
    }

    function getGreeting() public view returns (string memory) {
        return greeting;
    }

    function setGreeting(string memory _newGreeting) public {
        greeting = _newGreeting;
    }
}
Example

Deploy with constructor argument "Hello Cohortia Learners!" Then call getGreeting and setGreeting to observe differences between off-chain reads and state-changing transactions.

Remix steps
  1. Create Greeter.sol in File Explorer.
  2. Paste code and set pragma if needed.
  3. Open Solidity Compiler plugin and select matching version.
  4. Compile, then open Deploy & Run Transactions and choose JavaScript VM.
  5. Pass initial greeting as constructor argument and click deploy.
Common misconception: Calling getGreeting from the UI always costs gas. It does not when invoked as a view off-chain; only state-mutating calls cost gas.
Key Takeaway

Hands-on compilation, deployment, and interaction reveal how contract initialization and state changes actually behave on-chain.

screens.title: Deploying contracts in Remix (JavaScript VM)
screens.subtitle: From creating a file to observing transactions in the console

narration.text: Deploying in Remix is a predictable sequence that helps you iterate quickly without running a local node. First create a new. sol file in the File Explorer and paste your contract code. Second, open the Solidity Compiler and select the version that satisfies your pragma; compile until you see a green check. Third, open the Deploy & Run Transactions panel, set the Environment to JavaScript VM to simulate a blockchain in your browser, and input any constructor arguments. When you click deploy, Remix creates a deployment transaction visible in the panel and the browser console. Observe the gas used for deployment and any events or logs produced. After deployment, the contract appears under Deployed Contracts where you can call view functions and send transactions to mutating functions. A common misconception is that deployment to JavaScript VM emulates network latency and mining—it's immediate for quick testing but not identical to a real network. Key takeaway: use the JavaScript VM to validate behavior, then test on a testnet before mainnet deployment. Deploying contracts in Remix (JavaScript VM) means create file, compile with matching pragma, select javascript vm, deploy with constructor args, then interact and inspect transactions in the console.. In practical terms, from creating a file to observing transactions in the console. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Remix Deployment
Deploying to JavaScript VM
Step 1: Create Greeter.sol in File Explorer and paste code.
Step 2: Open Solidity Compiler, select version matching pragma, and compile.
Step 3: Open Deploy & Run Transactions, set Environment to JavaScript VM, pass constructor args, and deploy.

Constructor args must match types and be entered with correct syntax in the deploy field.
Deployment gas depends on contract size and constructor logic.
Key Takeaway

Use JavaScript VM for fast iteration, but validate on a testnet to approximate network behavior before production deployment.

screens.title: Integer overflows, underflows, and safety
screens.subtitle: Why Solidity 0.8.x changed behavior and what to watch for

narration.text: Integer overflow and underflow used to silently wrap around in older Solidity versions, causing severe vulnerabilities. From Solidity 0.8.0 onward, arithmetic operations revert on overflow and underflow by default, preventing this silent corruption. This shift changes how you reason about arithmetic in contracts. A concrete example: adding one to the maximum value of an unsigned integer previously wrapped to zero; with modern compilers the operation reverts and stops the transaction. A common misconception is that newer compilers remove the need for careful bounds checks entirely — they reduce accidental wraparound but you still must reason about limits, denominators, and safe divisions. When porting old code, verify whether libraries relied on wrapping behavior. For gas and safety, prefer explicit checks and consider open-source libraries only after understanding their assumptions. Key takeaway: use a compiler with overflow checks enabled, and audit arithmetic-heavy code paths to avoid edge-case failures or unexpected reverts during transactions. Integer overflows, underflows, and safety means solidity 0.8.x reverts on overflow/underflow by default; still audit arithmetic logic and ported code carefully.. In practical terms, why solidity 0.8.x changed behavior and what to watch for. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Overflow protection
keyIdea.text: Solidity 0.8.x reverts on overflow/underflow by default; still audit arithmetic logic and ported code carefully.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Overflow & Safety
Overflow behavior

Older Solidity allowed wrapping. From 0.8.0, arithmetic reverts on overflow and underflow by default. This prevents many classes of bugs but introduces potential reverts if bounds are overlooked.

Example: Adding 1 to the maximum uint256 now reverts instead of wrapping to zero.
Checklist when handling numbers
  • Confirm compiler version supports overflow checks.
  • Audit arithmetic-heavy code for edge cases and reverts.
  • When porting older contracts, search for reliance on wrap semantics.
Key Takeaway

Modern Solidity protects against wraparound; remain vigilant about bounds and ported code that expects wrapping.

These checks confirm your understanding of constructor timing, view semantics, and gas for state changes. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three essential concepts to carry forward. First, Solidity is a contract-oriented language that compiles into EVM bytecode; the way you write code affects gas and security because bytecode is what runs across all nodes. Second, the Remix IDE provides a rapid browser-based loop for creating files, selecting matching compiler versions via pragma, compiling, and deploying to a simulated JavaScript VM — perfect for early testing. Third, data types and variable scope matter: use uint for non-negative quantities like balances, address for Ethereum accounts, and prefer local variables and view functions when persistence is unnecessary to reduce gas. Remember the practical checks from the lab: confirm constructor initialization, call a view function to verify free reads, and perform a state-changing transaction to observe gas. Keeping these three ideas in mind will make your next contract safer, cheaper to run, and easier to debug.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Solidity → EVM, Remix for fast testing, and careful type and scope selection to manage gas and correctness.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Key Concepts
Solidity & EVM

Source compiles to bytecode; bytecode runs on the EVM and gas measures cost.

Remix IDE

Use the File Explorer, Compiler, and Deploy panels to iterate quickly and test contracts on a simulated VM.

Types & Scope

Choose types carefully (uint for balances, address for accounts) and minimize state writes in favor of local computation and view functions.

Summary Takeaway

Combine good type choices, a matching compiler, and minimal persistent state to build safer, more efficient contracts.

narration.text: Keep three quick reminders handy as you code. First, always match your pragma and compiler version to avoid surprising behavior. Second, remember the cost model: storage writes are costly and view reads are free off-chain. Third, pick types that express intent and avoid negative-value types for balances. When you return to coding, run the small Remix loop: edit, compile, deploy to JavaScript VM, call a view, then send a transaction — this confirms constructor initialization, read semantics, and gas for writes. These short checks will make your development cycles safer and more predictable.
